stages.title: Argument analysis
stages.hook: A friend says, "We should ban phones at school because they distract students." What exactly is the claim, and what is the reason?
explain: An argument is a set of statements in which some (premises) are offered as reasons to accept another (the conclusion). To analyse an argument, first find the conclusion, then the premises, then ask two questions: do the premises support the conclusion, and are the premises true?

Indicator words help: "therefore", "so", "thus" often signal a conclusion; "because", "since", "given that" signal premises. Arguments often hide an assumption, a missing premise that must be true for the reasoning to work. In "We should ban phones because they distract", the hidden premise is that distraction at school is harmful enough to justify a ban.

A deductive argument aims at certainty; an inductive one at probability. Strong inductive arguments make the conclusion likely; cogent ones are strong with true premises. To evaluate, look for weak links, missing premises, and counter-evidence. Standardising the argument (writing premises numbered then the conclusion) makes this easier.

example.q: "Our town needs a new library because many children have no books at home, and libraries lend books free." Standardise it.
steps: Conclusion: Our town needs a new library.
P1: Many children have no books at home.
P2: Libraries lend books free.
Hidden premise: a new library would reach those children.
example.a: C: the town needs a library; P1 and P2 support it, with a hidden premise about reaching the children.

analogies.city: A council says "Build the road because traffic is heavy". The hidden premise is that a road reduces traffic.
analogies.home: "Take an umbrella; the sky is dark." Hidden premise: dark skies mean rain.
analogies.tech: "Update the app since it has bugs." Hidden premise: the update fixes them.

stages.mnemonic: Find the Conclusion, number the Premises, hunt the Hidden gap.
terms: Premises offered as reasons for a conclusion.
An unstated premise needed for the argument to work.

misc.right: In logic, an argument is a set of reasons for a conclusion, not a fight.

stages.limits: Ordinary language is loose, so there may be several fair ways to read what an argument means.

trip.prompt: Find how the page defines premises, conclusion and the kinds of argument.

stages.title: Formal logic fundamentals
stages.hook: If "it is raining" and "it is cold" are both true, what about "it is raining or it is cold"? What about "it is raining and it is warm"?
explain: Formal logic studies the form of arguments using precise symbols. A proposition is a statement that is either true or false. We combine propositions with connectives: not (¬), and (∧), or (∨), if-then (→).

Truth tables list every combination of truth values. "P ∧ Q" is true only when both P and Q are true. "P ∨ Q" (inclusive or) is true when at least one is true. "¬P" flips the value. "P → Q" is false only when P is true and Q is false; otherwise it is true. For example, the promise "if you pass, I will buy you a book" is broken only if you pass and get no book.

Two statements are logically equivalent if they have the same truth table. An important equivalence is P → Q ≡ ¬Q → ¬P (the contrapositive). The converse, Q → P, is not equivalent. Necessary and sufficient conditions: in P → Q, P is sufficient for Q, and Q is necessary for P. De Morgan's laws: ¬(P ∧ Q) ≡ ¬P ∨ ¬Q and ¬(P ∨ Q) ≡ ¬P ∧ ¬Q.

example.q: Is "if P then Q" true when P is false and Q is true?
steps: Recall: the conditional is false only when P is true and Q is false.
Here P is false, so it is not that case.
So it is true.

analogies.home: "If the gate is open, the dog is out." The promise is broken only if the gate is open and the dog is not out.
analogies.tech: A login needs the right username AND the right password.
analogies.city: A shop accepts cash OR card.

stages.mnemonic: AND needs both, OR needs one, IF-THEN breaks on true-then-false.
terms: A statement that is either true or false.
True only when both parts are true.
False only when the first is true and the second false.

misc.wrong: "If P then Q" and "if Q then P" mean the same.
misc.right: They do not. The converse can be false when the original is true.

stages.limits: Formal logic captures only some everyday meanings; "if" in ordinary talk often means more than the logical conditional.

stages.title: Probability and uncertainty
stages.hook: A fair six-sided die is rolled. What is the chance of a 5? What if you roll twice and want two 5s?
explain: Probability measures how likely an event is on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). When all outcomes are equally likely, probability = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of outcomes. A fair die: P(5) = 1/6 ≈ 0.167.

Rules: the probabilities of all outcomes add to 1, so P(not A) = 1 − P(A). For independent events (one does not affect the other), P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). So two 5s in two rolls: 1/6 × 1/6 = 1/36. For mutually exclusive events, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B): a 5 or a 6 is 1/6 + 1/6 = 1/3.

Past results do not change the chance of independent events: after five heads in a row, a fair coin still has a 1/2 chance of heads next. Believing otherwise is the gambler's fallacy. Probabilities describe long-run frequencies or degrees of belief, and real-life uncertainty is often about incomplete information, not just chance.

example.q: A bag has 3 red and 5 blue marbles. You draw one without looking. What is P(red)? After replacing it, what is P(two reds in a row)?
steps: Total marbles: 8.
With replacement the draws are independent.

analogies.sport: A basketball player makes 70% of free throws; over many throws the share approaches 0.7.
analogies.nature: A forecast of 30% rain means that on days with such conditions, it rains about 3 days in 10.
analogies.home: Drawing a random sock from a drawer with 4 black and 6 white socks gives P(black) = 4/10.

stages.mnemonic: Probability: favourable over total; chances multiply for AND, add for OR.
terms: A number from 0 to 1 measuring how likely an event is.

The event "not A", with probability 1 − P(A).

misc.right: Each fair toss is independent. The coin has no memory.

stages.limits: Probability has several interpretations (frequency, belief), and real events seldom have perfectly known odds.

stages.title: Cognitive biases
stages.hook: A friend says flying is more dangerous than driving because plane crashes are in the news. Is the news a good guide to risk?
explain: Cognitive biases are systematic tendencies to think in ways that depart from careful reasoning. They come from mental shortcuts (heuristics) that are fast and often useful but sometimes mislead.

Some well-studied ones: confirmation bias (seeking and favouring information that supports what we already believe); availability heuristic (judging how common something is by how easily examples come to mind, so vivid news makes rare events seem common); anchoring (being swayed by a first number); hindsight bias ("I knew it all along"); the sunk-cost fallacy (continuing because of past investment); overconfidence (being more sure than our accuracy justifies); and framing effects (choices change with wording).

Knowing about biases does not make us immune. Helpful habits include seeking disconfirming evidence, considering base rates, getting an outside view, slowing down for important choices, and using checklists. Researchers also debate how irrational people really are, since shortcuts often work well in the environments we live in.

example.q: A shop shows "Was 100, now 60". Customers think 60 is a bargain. Which bias?
steps: The first number 100 sets a reference point.
It changes how we judge 60.
This is anchoring.

analogies.city: After seeing news of a rare event, people overestimate how often it happens.
analogies.sport: A fan remembers the wins of his team and forgets the losses.
analogies.tech: You keep a failing app project going because you already spent months on it.

stages.mnemonic: Biases are shortcuts that can trip: check them with a slow second look.

Favouring information that supports existing beliefs.
Judging likelihood by how easily examples come to mind.
Continuing because of past cost that cannot be recovered.

misc.right: Everyone has them, including experts. Being clever does not remove them, although awareness and good habits can reduce their effects.

stages.limits: Researchers debate how much human judgment is biased versus well adapted to real environments.

stages.title: Decision trees
stages.hook: You can take a safe prize of 50 coins, or flip a fair coin: heads gives 120 coins, tails gives 0. Which should you choose?
explain: A decision tree is a diagram that maps choices and what can happen after each. Square nodes are decisions, circles are chance events, and ends show outcomes with payoffs. Branches from a chance node carry probabilities that add up to 1.

To compare options, work backwards (right to left) and compute the expected value (EV): multiply each outcome's value by its probability and add. The coin gamble has EV = 0.5 × 120 + 0.5 × 0 = 60 coins, while the safe option is 50. Pure EV favours the gamble.

But EV is not the whole story. People differ in how much they dislike risk. If 50 coins covers an essential need, taking the sure thing may be wise. Costs, time, and probabilities that are only estimates also matter, so test how the decision changes when the numbers change (sensitivity analysis).

example.q: Option A: launch a stall for 200 coins cost, a 60% chance of earning 500 and 40% of earning 100 (before cost). Option B: do nothing (0). What is the EV of A (net)?
steps: B is 0.
example.a: Net EV of A is 140 coins, more than B.

analogies.farm: Plant a risky crop that earns a lot in good rain or little in drought, or a steady crop.
analogies.sport: A team decides whether to attack or defend depending on the chance of scoring.
analogies.city: Choose a route: a fast road that is sometimes jammed or a slower steady one.

stages.mnemonic: Branch, weigh by chance, add up: expected value wins the cup, but check the risk.
terms: A diagram of choices, chances and outcomes.
The probability-weighted average of the outcomes.
Preferring a sure outcome to a gamble of equal or higher expected value.

misc.wrong: The best option is always the one with the highest expected value.
misc.right: Expected value ignores risk attitude, one-off stakes and uncertain probabilities.

stages.limits: Real probabilities and payoffs are estimates, and many decisions have values that are not just money.

stages.title: Strategic planning
stages.hook: A school wants every pupil to read well in three years. What would you do first, next and later?
explain: Strategic planning is deciding where you want to go and how to get there, given limited resources. A common sequence: define a vision and clear goals; analyse the situation; generate options; choose; plan actions with owners, dates and resources; carry out; and review.

A SWOT analysis lists internal strengths and weaknesses and external opportunities and threats. Good goals are SMART: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. Scenario planning asks "what if?" for several possible futures so the plan still works if things change.

Strategy involves trade-offs: you cannot do everything, so you decide what not to do. Plans also need feedback loops, measures that show progress, so you can adapt. A plan that is never reviewed becomes outdated, and a plan that changes every week is no plan.

example.q: A community garden wants to supply vegetables to 50 families in a year. Make a SWOT and a goal.
steps: Strengths: many volunteers. Weaknesses: little money.
Opportunities: free seeds from a local group. Threats: drought.
Goal: by December, harvest 20 kg per family per year (measurable and time-bound).
example.a: SWOT identifies strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats; the SMART goal is measurable and time-bound.

analogies.farm: A farm plans crops by season, with a backup if the rains fail.
analogies.city: A city plans a new bus line using population growth forecasts.
analogies.sport: A club builds a squad over several seasons, not only the next match.

stages.mnemonic: SWOT the scene, SMART the goal, scenario for rain, review again.
terms: A plan of choices to reach long-term goals.

misc.wrong: A good plan covers every detail from the start.
misc.right: Plans should be clear on goals and flexible in details, since conditions change.

stages.limits: Strategy tools simplify; real organisations face uncertainty, politics and unknowns that tools cannot capture.

stages.title: Systems thinking
stages.hook: Why does a thermostat keep a room at a steady temperature? What happens if a system has a delay?
explain: Systems thinking looks at how parts connect and interact to produce behaviour of the whole. Instead of asking only "what caused this event?" it asks what structure keeps producing this pattern.

Key ideas: elements, connections and purpose. Feedback loops are central. A balancing (negative) loop pushes a system back towards a target, like a thermostat. A reinforcing (positive) loop amplifies change, like compound interest or a snowball. Delays between action and effect can cause overshoot and oscillation: if a shower takes a while to warm, you may turn the tap too far and swing between cold and hot.

Systems have unintended consequences: fixing one part may shift the problem elsewhere. Stocks (amounts that accumulate, like water in a bath) change through flows (inflow and outflow). To change a system, look for leverage points where small changes have big effects, and try small experiments before large changes.

example.q: A bathtub has 100 litres. Inflow is 15 litres per minute and outflow is 10 litres per minute. How much water after 6 minutes?
steps: Net flow: 15 − 10 = +5 litres per minute.
Change in 6 min: 6 × 5 = 30 litres.
Stock: 100 + 30 = 130 litres.

analogies.home: A thermostat switches heating on and off to hold a set temperature (balancing loop).
analogies.nature: More rabbits lead to more foxes, which lead to fewer rabbits (balancing loops with delay).
analogies.city: More roads can bring more cars, which fill the roads again (a reinforcing loop).

stages.mnemonic: Stocks fill, flows pour, loops steer, delays shake, leverage points are where you make the change.
terms: Parts connected so that they work together as a whole.
A chain in which an output affects its own input.
An accumulated amount and the rates that change it.
A place where a small change causes a large effect.

misc.wrong: In a complex system, one cause leads to one effect.
misc.right: Effects often have several causes, loops and delays, so results can be surprising.

stages.limits: Models of systems are simplifications; real systems cross boundaries and can behave unpredictably.

trip.prompt: Find examples of feedback loops on the page.

questions.q: A thermostat is an example of...
o: A balancing loop
A reinforcing loop
A stock
A delay only
questions.why: It pushes temperature back to the target.

questions.q: Compound interest on savings is an example of...
o: A reinforcing loop
A balancing loop that pulls back to a target
A delay between an action and its effect
A leverage point where small push has large effect

questions.q: A tank has 200 litres, inflow 8 litres/min and outflow 12 litres/min. How many litres after 10 minutes?
questions.why: Net flow is −4 per minute, so 10 min gives −40 and 200 − 40 = 160.

questions.q: Why can delays cause overshoot?
o: We keep acting before we see the effect
Delays remove the feedback from the system
Delays stop all change from happening
Delays make every system more stable
questions.why: Corrections pile up before results show.

questions.q: What is a stock in systems thinking?
o: An amount that accumulates
A rate of change over time
A goal that the system is aiming for
A type of shop that sells goods
questions.why: Stocks are levels like water or population.

questions.q: A city builds a wider road and traffic soon returns. What does this suggest?
o: The fix triggered a response that undid the benefit
New roads can never be built in cities
Traffic is fixed and cannot ever change
The road was still too narrow after all

questions.q: Why make small experiments in a complex system?
o: To learn about responses with low risk
To slow down progress on purpose
Because it is always easy to change things
To avoid the need for thinking

questions.q: Match each concept to an example.
questions.why: Each is a core system idea.

questions.q: Put the systems analysis steps in order.
items: Define the system and its purpose

questions.q: Explain why a quick fix can make a problem worse in a system.
questions.model: The fix may trigger feedback or shift the problem elsewhere, so the benefit is undone or new problems appear later.

panel.q: Which is a likely sign of a reinforcing loop?
o: Growth that speeds up on itself
Steady return to a fixed target level
No change at all over a long time
A single event that never repeats

panel.q: Explain how a balancing loop keeps a room at a set temperature.
panel.model: The thermostat measures the temperature and compares it to the target, turning heating on when it is too cold and off when it is warm enough, pushing the temperature back to the target.

panel.q: Why is it useful to ask for the structure behind repeated events?
o: Structure produces the pattern, so fixing events alone may not help
Events never repeat in any system
Structure is not relevant to what happens
Only the events themselves ever matter

teach.model: Systems thinking studies how parts connect. Stocks change through flows. Balancing loops steer towards a target and reinforcing loops amplify change. Delays cause overshoot. Fixes can have unintended effects, so look for leverage points and test small changes.

stages.title: Metacognition
stages.hook: You re-read your notes five times and feel ready, but you fail the quiz. Why did your feeling of knowing mislead you?
explain: Metacognition is thinking about your own thinking: knowing what you know, judging how well you are learning, and choosing how to study. It includes monitoring (checking your understanding) and control (changing your strategy).

Our feelings about learning are often wrong. Re-reading feels easy because the text looks familiar, which creates an illusion of knowing. Studies show that retrieval practice (testing yourself), spacing (spreading study over days) and interleaving (mixing different problem types) usually give stronger long-term learning than re-reading or cramming, even though they feel harder. Difficulties that help learning are called desirable difficulties.

Memory also has limits that metacognition must respect. We forget quickly without review (the forgetting curve). Memories are reconstructed, so false memories can form, and confidence is only a weak guide to accuracy: people can be very sure and wrong. Brain-training games improve performance on the trained tasks, but evidence for broad gains in general intelligence is weak.

example.q: You must learn 20 vocabulary words. Compare two plans: (A) read the list 5 times tonight; (B) test yourself on 20 words on three separate days. Which is better and why?
steps: Plan A makes words feel familiar (illusion of knowing).
Plan B forces recall and spaces it out.
So B builds stronger, longer-lasting memory.
example.a: Plan B, because retrieval and spacing strengthen memory more than re-reading.

analogies.sport: An athlete records her times to know honestly how she is improving, not just how she feels.
analogies.music: A pianist mixes scales, pieces and sight-reading (interleaving) instead of one for an hour.
analogies.home: Cover a recipe and try to say the steps before checking, instead of just looking at it.

stages.mnemonic: Test, space, mix, then check: knowing what you know, with no wreck.
terms: Awareness and control of your own thinking and learning.
Learning by recalling information from memory.
Mixing different topics or problem types in practice.
Feeling you know something because it looks familiar.

misc.wrong: If I feel confident, I have learned it.
misc.right: Confidence and accuracy are only loosely linked. Test yourself to find out.

stages.limits: Study techniques work on average. Individual results vary, and "learning styles" matching has not been supported by good evidence.

trip.prompt: See how the page links metacognition to learning strategies.

questions.q: What is metacognition?
o: Thinking about your own thinking
A kind of memory loss in old age
A method of reading very fast
A type of school test
questions.why: It means monitoring and controlling your learning.

questions.q: Which method usually gives the strongest long-term memory?
o: Testing yourself over several days
Re-reading the notes once more
Highlighting the key lines only
Cramming everything the night before

questions.q: Why does re-reading create an illusion of knowing?
o: The text feels familiar, which feels like understanding
It makes the text look different each time
The text is too hard to read twice
It forces your mind to use retrieval

questions.q: What is interleaving?
o: Mixing different topics or types in practice
Studying one topic for hours without a change
Skipping practice on hard topics
Reading each topic aloud to a friend
questions.why: It helps you choose the right method.

questions.q: A witness is 100% sure of a detail that a video shows is wrong. What does this show?
o: Confidence is not a guarantee of accuracy
Videos always lie about what happened
Witnesses never remember anything
Confidence is always a sign of being right
questions.why: Memories can be wrong yet feel certain.

o: People can remember events that did not happen
Only liars ever have false memories
They never occur in real life
They are always easy to spot

o: There is little good evidence that they do beyond the trained tasks
Yes, strongly, for almost all people
Yes, for everyone who plays them
They can replace the sleep you need
questions.why: Gains often do not transfer broadly.

questions.q: You plan to review a topic after 1 day, 3 days and 7 days from the first study day. On which day number is the last review if the first study is day 0?
questions.why: The last review is 7 days after day 0, which is day 7.

questions.q: Match each technique to what it does.
Explain why a study method that feels harder can lead to better learning.
questions.model: The extra effort of recalling or switching topics strengthens memory pathways, so learning lasts longer, although it feels less smooth than re-reading.

panel.q: A student scores well on a practice test the day after cramming but forgets most a month later. What does this show?
o: Cramming gives short-term performance but weak long-term memory
Tests are useless for measuring memory
Memory never fades with time
The test was simply too easy that day

panel.q: Why should you not rely only on how confident you feel to decide if you have learned something?
panel.model: Feeling confident can come from familiarity rather than real recall, so you should test yourself to check accuracy.

panel.q: A game claims to "boost your intelligence" in 10 minutes a day. What is the best response?
o: Look for independent evidence of wide gains beyond the game
Believe it at once and start playing
Trust the maker, who knows best
Play it even more each day
panel.why: Transfer to general ability is not well supported.

teach.model: Metacognition means knowing and controlling your own learning. Feelings of knowing can mislead, so test yourself, spread study over days and mix topics. Memories fade and can be false, and confidence does not guarantee accuracy.

stages.title: Game theory fundamentals
stages.hook: Two suspects are questioned separately. Each can stay silent or blame the other. What would you do, and what would you want the other person to do?
explain: Game theory studies strategic choices when the outcome for each player depends on everyone's choices. A game has players, strategies and payoffs. We often show a two-player game in a payoff matrix.

The prisoner's dilemma is the classic example. If both stay silent, each gets a light sentence (say 1 year). If both blame the other, each gets 3 years. If one blames and the other is silent, the blamer goes free (0) and the silent one gets 5. Whatever the other does, blaming is better for you (a dominant strategy), so both blame and get 3 years each, worse than the 1 year each from both staying silent. Individual rationality can produce a collectively worse result.

A Nash equilibrium is a set of strategies where nobody can gain by changing their own strategy alone. In the dilemma, (blame, blame) is the equilibrium. In repeated games, cooperation can arise: strategies like tit-for-tat (start cooperating, then copy the other player's last move) reward cooperation and punish betrayal. Not all games are zero-sum; many have gains from cooperation.

example.q: In a payoff matrix, you choose Cooperate or Defect. If both Cooperate: 3 each. Both Defect: 1 each. You Defect, they Cooperate: 5 for you, 0 for them. Is Defect dominant?
steps: If they Cooperate: Defect gives 5, Cooperate gives 3. So Defect is better.
If they Defect: Defect gives 1, Cooperate gives 0. So Defect is better.
Defect is better in both cases.
example.a: Yes, Defect is a dominant strategy, yet both Defecting gives 1 each, less than 3 each.

analogies.sport: Two teams both skip a costly rule, hoping for an edge, and end up worse off.
analogies.farm: Neighbouring farmers share a well: each over-uses it, then the well runs dry.
analogies.city: Two shops cut prices to win customers and both lose profit.

stages.mnemonic: Best for me whatever you do, yet worse for both of us too: the dilemma.
terms: A table showing each player's outcome for each strategy pair.
A strategy that is best whatever others do.
A situation where no one gains by changing alone.
A game in which one player's gain equals another's loss.

misc.wrong: Rational players always end up with the best result for everyone.
misc.right: In the prisoner's dilemma, rational individual choices produce a worse result for both than cooperation.

stages.limits: Real people often cooperate more than the simple model predicts, and many real situations have communication, trust and repeated contact that change the game.

trip.prompt: Look at the payoff table and the idea of iterated games.

questions.q: What is a dominant strategy?
o: One that is best whatever the others do
One that is the most popular among players
One that always wins the whole game
One that is kept hidden from others
questions.why: It beats the alternatives in every case.

questions.q: In the standard prisoner's dilemma, what do rational individuals choose?
o: Defect (blame)
Cooperate (silence)
Random
Nothing

questions.q: Why is mutual defection worse than mutual cooperation?
o: Both get a lower payoff
One of them gets a much higher payoff
Both of them go free in the end
The two results are exactly the same
questions.why: Each is worse off than with cooperation.

questions.q: What is a Nash equilibrium?
o: No player can gain by changing alone
Everyone ends up equally rich
The outcome with the highest total payoff
A fair draw between the two players
questions.why: It is a stable combination of strategies.

questions.q: What is tit-for-tat?
o: Cooperate first, then copy the opponent's last move
Always defect from the very first round
Always cooperate whatever the opponent does
Choose each move completely at random
questions.why: It rewards cooperation and punishes betrayal.

questions.q: Why might cooperation succeed in a repeated game?
o: Future rounds make betrayal costly
Players forget what happened before
There are no payoffs in later rounds
The rules force everyone to cooperate
questions.why: The shadow of the future matters.

questions.q: Two players each have 3 strategies. How many strategy pairs are in the payoff matrix?
Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: One's gain is the other's loss
The value of an outcome to a player

questions.q: Put the steps of analysing a simple game in order.
items: Write the payoffs in a matrix

questions.q: Explain why two farmers sharing a water source may overuse it even though both would do better by conserving.
questions.model: Each farmer gains by using more whatever the other does, but if both overuse the source runs dry and both lose, which is a prisoner's dilemma.
questions.why: Individual incentives conflict with the group.

panel.q: In a payoff matrix, strategy A gives you 4 or 2 and strategy B gives you 3 or 1 against the opponent's two choices (same order). Which is dominant?
o: A
B
Neither
Both
panel.why: A is higher in each column (4 > 3 and 2 > 1).

panel.q: How can communities or rules help avoid a prisoner's dilemma outcome?
panel.model: Agreements, rules, repeated contact and reputation can change the payoffs so that cooperation pays more than defecting.

panel.q: Which is a zero-sum game?
o: A single match with one winner and one loser
Two farms sharing one harvest road
Trade that helps both sides to gain
A team project where all work together
panel.why: One side's gain is the other's loss.

teach.model: Game theory studies strategic choices where outcomes depend on what everyone chooses. In the prisoner's dilemma, defecting is dominant, but both defecting is worse than both cooperating. A Nash equilibrium is a combination where no one gains by changing alone. Repeated play and rules can support cooperation.
